title: AM-GM for two variables
text:
Theorem 1 (AM-GM) For a, b \ge 0, \dfrac{a+b}{2} \ge \sqrt{ab}.







NoteSolution





Since (\sqrt a - \sqrt b)^2 \ge 0, expanding gives a + b \ge 2\sqrt{ab}. \square

title: MATHHHH
text:
Suppose V is a vector space such that dim(V) >= 2. If F is infinite prove that V can not be union of finitely many proper subspaces.






NoteSolution





Suppose for the sake of contradiction that V can be written as union of finitely many proper subspaces. Then V we can remove the subspaces that are subsets of each other and conclude that V can be writter as: V = U_1 \cup U_2 \cup ... \cup U_k where U_i \nsubseteq \bigcup_{j \neq i} U_j for all i, where U_i are proper subspaces of V. Choose u \in U_1 s.t u \notin \bigcup_{i=2}^{k}U_i. Because U_1 is proper subspace of V, there exist some v \in V-U_1. Consider the vectors u+tv where t \in F. if t \neq 0 then u+tv \notin U_1. We claim that for all U_i, i>1, at most one of the vectors u+tv are in U_i. Suppose for the sake of contradiction that u+t_1v, u+t_2v \in U_i. Then: (t_1-t_2)v \in U_i \implies v \in U_i \implies u \in U_i which is a contradiction. Because there are finitely many u+tv in U_1 \cup U_2 \cup ... \cup U_k but the number of vectors in the form u+tv is infinite, thus there exists some u+t^*v \notin U_1 \cup U_2 \cup ... \cup U_k = V which is a contradiction

title: LA P2
text:
Suppose V is finite dimensional vector space and T: V -> V is a linear map such that {v, T(v), ..., T^{(n-1)}(v)} is a basis for V. If S: V -> V is a linear transformation such that ST = TS, prove that S(x) = a_0I + a_1T(x) + ... + a_nT^{(n-1)}(x) for some a_i






NoteSolution





Suppose S(v) = a_0 v + a_1 T(v) + ... + a_n T(v)^{(n-1)} we claim that the a_i satisfy S(x) = a_0 v + a_1 T(x) + ... + a_n T(x)^{(n-1)}. Let P(x) = S(x) = a_0 v + a_1 T(x) + ... + a_n T(x)^{(n-1)}. By definition of a_i, we have P(v) = S(v). Because ST = TS, we obtain that ST^k = T^kS. Also because P is a polynomial of T, thus PT^k = T^KP. Thus we have P(T^k(v)) = T^k(P(V)) = T^k(S(v)) = S(T^k(v)). Because {v, Tv, T^2v, ..., T^{(n-1)v}} is a basis for V and P and S have the same outputs, thus S = P.
